To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
defective interfering (DI) particles of Sindbis (SINV) are readily produced in chicken or hamsters cells but are not produced by serial undiluted passages in mosquito cells.
defective interfering particles (DIPs) of Sindbis virus (SINV), generated in hamster (BHK) or chicken (CEF) cells, do not interfere with SINV replication in mosquito cells.

defective interfering particles (DI particles) of Sindbis virus, which are readily produced in chicken embryo fibroblast (CEF) and BHK-21 cell cultures, are silent or inert when tested in Aedes albopicus cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the replication of Sindbis virus in A. albopticus cells.
the development and use of Sindbis virus as a vector for the expression of foreign genes in Aedes albipictus cells.
the production and properties of defective interfering particles (DIP) of Sindbis virus (SINV).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Sindbis virus defective interfering particles are not produced in Aedes albipictus cells.
Sindbis virus defective interfering particles produced in chicken embryo fibroblast cells are not active in Aedes albipictus cells.
defective interfering particles are not generated in the A. albopicitus cell line.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Sindbis virus defective interfering particles generated by the methods of serial undilution passage in either BHK-21 or chicken embryo fibrobasts are silent or inert when tested in Aedes albopicus cells.
defective interfering particles generated in BHK or CE cells are not able to affect viral replication or the pattern of intracelluar RNA synthesis in A. alboptus cells.
defective interfering particles generated in one cell type are silent or inert when tested in a second cell type.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of defective interfering particles as antiviral agents in mosquito cells is not a viable strategy for the control of arthropod-borne viral disease.
the production of defective interfering particles in Sindbis virus-infected cells is dependent upon the cell type used for virus growth.

the Sindbis virus defective-interfering particles generated in chicken or mouse cells do not interfere in mosquito cell culture, which is a major obstacle for using these particles in the development of a live virus vaccine against mosquito-borne arboviruses.
